evidence.note: Claim: a suite waiter at the head of the queue is bounced by [ci].suite_wait_s the instant it reaches the head, because the give-up budget counts the whole time since queueing (suitelock.hold anchors it at start). Refuting observation: a waiter placed in line behind another ('ahead') past the budget, then at the head, gives up at line-time-only. Mechanism: give-up anchor is start (queue entry), not head arrival. Ran: uv run pytest tests/test_gate_run_timeout_suite_lock_wait.py::test_a_waiter_that_reaches_the_head_restarts_its_wait_budget -> FAILED on unfixed (gave up after 1.00s < 1.5, position 1) / PASSED on fixed.
ddflow brief --item fix-B-suite-wait-expires-at-head-of-queue; read the rules governing the suite-lock files (r-gemini-key-load for reviews) and prior lessons (Ba5d5d63f12 suite-lock override tests).

Implemented in the worktree: ddflow/services/suitelock.py hold() now anchors the give-up budget at head_since (first time the waiter reaches the head); regression test in tests/test_gate_run_timeout_suite_lock_wait.py. Committed 5c34c0223. Globs widened via ddflow update.

chunk_findings.detail: The new `anchor = head_since if head_since is not None else start` breaks the function’s documented contract that `wait_s` (from `ddflow ci run --timeout N`) bounds the queue wait. With `wait_s=10`, a run that queues at position #7 and reaches the head at t=9.9s while no suite slot is free sets `head_since=9.9`, so the expiration check won’t fire until t≈19.9s. The run can therefore spend nearly `2 * wait_s` in the queue even though `--timeout 10` is still documented as an upper bound on queue wait; this is the input that makes the change wrong.

chunk_findings.detail: The key assertion `busy.value.waited_s >= 1.5` only proves the waiter survived at least 1.5 s total; it does not prove the wait budget restarted when the waiter reached the head. A broken fix that merely adds a fixed 0.5 s delay before raising `SuiteBusy` (or otherwise extends the old whole-wait deadline by 0.5 s) would yield `waited_s == 1.5` and still `position == 1` after the 0.75 s fake line time, passing this test while still counting line time toward the budget.

data.probe: Intended: B-suite-wait-expires-at-head-of-queue changes the contract Ba5d5d63f12 stated. The give-up budget now bounds time pushed: the in-line leg (behind other waiters) and the at-head leg each capped at wait_s, so the total is bounded (<2*wait_s); the at-head leg is further bounded by the holder's finite run (its flock frees on completion or death). The bug's own requested fix is 'a waiter that is next should keep its place'. test_a_wait_override_extends_the_suite_wait_knob still gives up after wait_s for a waiter at the head from t=0, so the override bound is intact.

chunk_findings.detail: The new `anchor = head_since if head_since is not None else start` applies the head-arrival reset to *all* wait limits, including an explicit `wait_s` passed from `ddflow ci run --timeout N`. That breaks the function’s own documented contract at line ~230 that the per-run override “bounds the queue wait too”. Concrete failure: with `wait_s=1` (via `--timeout 1`), a run queued at position 2 at `t=0` reaches the head at `t=0.9` and the slot stays busy until `t=1.5`. The new code uses `head_since=0.9`, so it does not time out at `t=1.0`; it can break and start the run at `t=1.5` (or later), exceeding the caller’s 1-second queue-wait bound. The default `suite_wait_s` bug fix should not silently relax the explicit per-run override in the process.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/suitelock.py:267

chunk_findings.detail: The same `wait` value is both `[ci].suite_wait_s` and the per-run `wait_s` override, and the new `anchor = head_since` restart applies to both. The docstring above still promises that `ddflow ci run --timeout N` bounds queue wait in either direction (Ba5d5d63f12). Given `hold(..., wait_s=60)`, a waiter queued at t=0 who first sees `position == 1` at t=50 while the slot stays busy does not give up at t=60: `head_since` is 50, so `time.monotonic() - anchor >= wait` fires only at t=110. Total queue time is almost `2 * N`, so a shorter `--timeout` no longer caps the wait.
